params.let: '' if a == 1 else ('-' if a == -1 else str(a))

stem: The parabola $g$ is given by $y = {=ac}x^2 {=qs}{=qa}$. For what values of $x$ is $g$ {=word}?
solution: A parabola of the form $y = ax^2 + q$ has its turning point on the $y$-axis, at $(0, q)$. Here $q = {=q}$, so the turning point is $(0, {=q})$.
Here $a = {=a}$, which is {=sgn}, so the parabola opens {=opens} and the turning point is a {=ext}.
To the left of the turning point ($x \leq 0$) the graph is {=lw}. To the right of the turning point ($x \geq 0$) the graph is {=rw}.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Chooses the wrong side of the turning point
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student picks x ≤ 0 where x ≥ 0 is right, or the reverse. Either they ignore the sign of a (assuming every parabola rises to the right of the turning point) or they mix up increasing and decreasing.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Treats q as an x-value
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student thinks the turning point of y = ax^2 + q sits at x = q (reading it as (q, 0)), so they start the interval at x = q instead of x = 0. The constant q shifts the graph up or down, not left or right.

proposed_misconceptions.label: Gives the range instead of the x-values where the graph rises or falls
proposed_misconceptions.description: The student answers with the y-values the graph takes (y ≥ q or y ≤ q) when asked for the values of x where it is increasing or decreasing.

notes: Basic entry point, modelled on the book's ex6-3-7d (where is g increasing, solution: it increases from the turning point, x ≥ 0). The book reads a graph; here the equation y = ax^2 + q is given, and the same reasoning is used: find the turning point (0, q), then say on which side the graph rises. The sign of a is varied (a from -5 to 5, never 0) and the question alternates between increasing and decreasing, so the correct answer is x ≥ 0 in some instances and x ≤ 0 in others; the skeleton is the same. The turning point is included in the interval (x ≥ 0, x ≤ 0), as in the book's key; no distractor uses a strict inequality, so no option is correct under a second reading. q is never 0, so the 'shift-on-x' distractor (boundary q) always differs from the correct boundary 0. The inequality symbols come from small tables of unicode characters (≤, ≥) in let params, and the coefficient is written without a 1 when a = ±1 (ac table).
